extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of philosophy and psychology
extracted.subtask_description: Lecture-style exposition contrasting abstract/absolutist philosophy with Fechner's concrete, analogical approach; discusses qualities that make metaphysical or philosophical writing (and visionary description) persuasive and alive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concreteness ('thickness') vs thinness
rubrics_metrics.description: The lecture praises 'thickness' — 'the intense concreteness of Fechner, his fertility of detail' — and criticises transcendental/absolutist systems as 'thin', 'abstract', 'indigent', 'threadbare' and 'school-room' in appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concrete, detail-rich argument and description over purely abstract, formal or 'jejune' categories. The author gives as anti-examples writers who present only a 'pure abstraction' or 'timeless soap-bubble' and who fail to 'thicken' their schemes with particulars. Concrete particulars should be used to make abstract claims intelligible and persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analogy while accounting for differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Fechner 'makes difference and analogy walk abreast' — analogical reasoning is central but must not neglect differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using analogy (e.g., to argue for higher minds or world-souls), explicitly note where the analogy breaks down; avoid projecting human particulars literally onto non-human or divine subjects. Treat analogy as a guide, not a literal mapping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cumulative effect through multitude of concrete points
rubrics_metrics.description: Fechner's power is 'due altogether to the profuseness of his concrete imagination, to the multitude of the points which he considers successively, to the cumulative effect of his learning... and of the ingenuity of his detail.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build persuasive conviction by assembling many varied, concrete considerations and small examples rather than relying on a single abstract proof. Thoroughness and an accumulation of particulars strengthen a speculative claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homely, vernacular style and readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Fechner is praised for an 'admirably homely style, of the vernacular sort.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear, accessible, colloquial (but well-crafted) prose increases the appeal and persuasive force of philosophical or visionary writing. Avoid over-formal or obscure diction that distances readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and speaking as one having authority (authentic vision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fechner 'speaks as one having authority, and not as if he were one of the common herd of professorial philosophic scribes.' His sincerity and directness are emphasized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authenticity — writing that conveys first-hand perception, conviction, and moral/psychological sincerity — is judged valuable. Present claims as grounded in seeing or experience where appropriate, rather than merely repeating second-hand doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vision and enthusiasm as complements to reason
rubrics_metrics.description: James notes that 'vision and faith must eke [reason] out' and that 'where there is no vision the people perish.' Vision/enthusiasm matter where abstract methods leave gaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow room for imaginative vision and vital enthusiasm in accounts of reality; they can supply the lived, affective content that purely rationalistic methods fail to provide. But they should complement, not replace, careful argument and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer empirical/scientific methods over abstract dialectic
rubrics_metrics.description: James observes that in science 'hypotheses, and deductions from these, controlled by sense-observations and analogies with what we know elsewhere, are to be thanked for all of science's results.' Fechner used such methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground speculative claims in observation, testable hypotheses, and analogies tied to empirical facts rather than relying solely on dialectical/mystical proofs. Give examples and observable correlates for metaphysical claims when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid metaphysical overreach and encyclopedic explicitness
rubrics_metrics.description: The absolute is criticized for requiring an 'infinite atmosphere of explicit negativity' and being obliged to be 'articulately aware' of countless trivial negations; such features render it 'irrational' or implausible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of ontologies that demand an implausible burden of explicit content or knowledge (e.g., that an ultimate mind must literally register every negation about every thing). Keep metaphysical claims parsimonious and avoid needless metaphysical baggage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate passion with logic ('shall-be' temper)
rubrics_metrics.description: James criticizes the monistic 'shall-be' temper: 'Unity is good, therefore things shall cohere; they shall be one; there shall be categories ...' and warns that Hegel confuses logic with passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let evaluative desires (what ought to be) masquerade as logical proof. Distinguish normative urges and aesthetic preferences from argument and evidence; resist forcing coherence because unity is prized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marks for ascribing higher/superior consciousness (worldbuilding criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: To argue the earth's superiority/animacy Fechner adduces marks like 'independence of other external beings', 'complexity in unity', 'to develop from within', and 'individuality of type' as signs of higher rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When hypothesizing or depicting non-human or planetary consciousness in fiction or philosophy, plausibly attribute properties such as relative independence, large-scale integrative complexity, internal development, and distinct individuality to make the claim credible to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sensory-rich imagery to make abstractions vivid
rubrics_metrics.description: James reproduces Fechner's luminous evocation of the earth: 'a shining ball, sky-blue and sun-lit... reflecting the heavens from all her waters... myriads of lights and shadows...' as evidence of the power of vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ vivid, multi-sensory description to personify or render abstract wholes convincing. Concrete imagery can convert an abstract thesis into an emotionally resonant experience for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance abstraction with particulars; avoid unsupported 'implicit presence' claims
rubrics_metrics.description: James faults doctrines that claim the whole of reality is 'implicitly present' in finite experiences without showing mediation or particulars; such claims are 'thin' and unpersuasive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting sweeping metaphysical claims, provide mediating particulars or mechanisms that show how the general is present in the particular; avoid relying on the single label 'implicit' without explanatory detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy limits: avoid expecting literal anatomical correspondences
rubrics_metrics.description: When asked 'where are her brain and nerves?' Fechner (via James) answers that expecting literal brain-like organs in the earth is a mistake; functions may be performed in different ways at different scales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not demand literal one-to-one analogues between human anatomy/psychology and other orders of being. Instead, seek functional or structural analogues appropriate to scale and context, and explain how those different mechanisms achieve analogous results.
